utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my view afterwards being -- since I became a seasoned inmate, if I might call myself that, this contained the name of the detainee, that is his first name and last name and, what shall I say, a reference. That is, it presumably said who was guilty of what. In those early interrogations, that is my view. They put an evaluation, an evaluation of -- personal evaluation, that is, people who had been interrogated and taken to the police as the four of us were, and then an opinion about them was put down on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But how could they give a personal evaluation about you as you were not interrogated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you because you tell us it was a personal evaluation so what could they tell you when nobody talked with you there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose they thought I was not important until -- since they did not interrogate me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, were people's names in dormitories taken down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did they know who was in which dormitory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But then who took those names and what did they take down?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frequently, Kajin, especially, that is, that stuck in my memory, they would take out all the inmates for some kind of roll-calls, for some list read-outs, I'm not sure what it was. But many inmates were killed during evening roll-calls, following lists. I suppose lists, I suppose, the lists had the names of people who were not there, who were missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time that you mention that all detainees were taken out. Why did you remember it now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is the first time that somebody's asking me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, wouldn't one think of it even without being asked? I mean, when one thinks about what went on in the camp --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not think it important, nor did anyone ask me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So there were -- there wasn't taking down of names in dormitories, did they exist or didn't they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: How should I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that attempts were made to establish roughly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of detainees and whether they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived how many rooms were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only two, dormitories 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said that you decided that Room 1 was better for you than Room 2. Does that mean --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you could change the room in which you were without asking anyone, without seeking any permission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, it sounds a bit odd, in view of what you are telling us about that place. It means that people could of their own will just move from room to room.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why should it be odd? Of 1200 or 1300 inmates, they simply could not keep an eye on all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And when you moved, were there 1200, 1300, or how many?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at that time there were much less, much less. There could have been about 400 or 500 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you said that there were about 60 when you arrived.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say there were 600, how could I know? I can tell you roughly 400 or 500, but it could be 600.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, how do you make these assessments, 400 or 600?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Simply. When I arrived about one-third of the camp was full. When there was the largest number of detainees, then we were about 1300, 1400, so that is how I roughly tried to assess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned some searchlights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When and where were those searchlights placed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The searchlights were placed at a rather late date. I cannot remember when that was exactly, but say towards the closure of the camp, perhaps some 20 days before it -- in the latter half of my detention. They did not exist in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the usher please put on the ELMO Exhibit 2E?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you see those searchlights in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You can't?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't, not on this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Just leave the photograph there. Will you please leave the photograph there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you now, please, put your drawing on the ELMO? I do not know the number, the number of the drawing. I apologise. Thank you. And where are the searchlights on this drawing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, right, so here, on this sketch, in the corner, that is where I drew them, in front of dormitories 1 and 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was: Where are the searchlights? So tell me where is the searchlight on this picture here that we have on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. He's drawn it on the plan, so he's told us where it is, Mr. Petrovic. There is no need to go over it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, yes. Something is drawn and it is marked as "searchlights" but not to the two lampposts which existed there before, before the armed conflict, which were still there during the armed conflict and which still are there -- which are still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question is: Where are they, because this is rather a detailed sketch?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lampposts have nothing to do with the searchlights. As there were no -- as they were -- as their lights were never on, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on. Then tell us very briefly, these searchlights, at what height were they mounted? What kind of bulbs did they have? What was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly what type of bulbs they had. I know they were mobile. That is, those were searchlights which had been brought there at a later date. In the beginning they were roughly one searchlight per two dormitories but, later on, both searchlights were directed more or less at Room 3, at dormitory 3. I think they had a special source of energy, as far as I can remember. I'm not sure about that. But I know they put them there later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said much later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, some 20 days or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to go back, very briefly, to food and water, which was supplied in Keraterm. Who supplied it? What kind of means of transportation were used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, food was delivered in a yellow, small TAM truck, and water later on -- oh, dear, what was that? I think for a while, it was an army cistern, and later on, I think a civilian one, I think so. Well, at least it wasn't olive-green grey.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How do you know that? Who sliced the bread that was brought?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inmates could apply or those whom they choose -- chose.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, something about the security. Did you ever see anyone but guards on duty doing the security job?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Lamentably, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Whom did you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. I'm not asking you about your opinion. I'm asking you about your recollection.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is the same, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, not quite.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my recollection is that anyone could come to the camp, that is, any Serb could come, whether in a uniform or not, and they did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any military police units in the neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly behind, behind the dormitories. That is something I heard. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned Zivko Knezevic several times, and you said that he was the commander during the first ten days or so which means, if my calculation is good, around the 22nd?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that he was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very simply. On the basis of the behaviour of shift leaders and other guards, when a car bringing in the camp commander would come, be that Knezevic or Sikirica, they behaved differently. They either forced us to go back into the rooms or something. At any rate, we could see by their behaviour that the camp commander was on his way.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The other day you used the word "awe". Was Zeljko Knezevic viewed with awe?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, you could also say that, or respect, or awe. But be that as it may, they would start behaving differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see Knezevic's orders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, mostly around that reception hut. That is where he would come to speak to shift leaders or guards. He never came near the dormitories.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you mentioned that you used the telephone on one occasion. Where was that telephone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that reception office, to call it that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really remember, but I know that a friend of mine was on guard duty, my best man's kum. And my brother called me during that period of time, and then he came to fetch me and I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand. Did your brother call you or did you call him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. He called my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And who is this man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you no problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Do you want to go into closed session to give us the name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Perhaps. Perhaps it would be better.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right so could we go into closed session for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You said several times that some orders were given from the weigh hut. Did you hear them? Do you know the contents of the conversations? Did you hear what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How long were the shifts in Keraterm in the early days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the early days, as far as I can remember, they were from 6.00 to 3.00. Afterwards --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: My question was in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from 6.00 to 3.00, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And then the next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: And then the next from 3.00 to 11.00 maybe, and then from 10.00 to 6.00 again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And at a later stage?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At a later stage they were 12-hour shifts, that is 6.00 to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: There were three shifts, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And throughout your detention in Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On Thursday you mentioned Tomo Prodan's shift. What shift was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that he was there replacing somebody. I'm not sure, but I know that the second time they took me out, it was owing to these men that my life was saved by accident.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I understand well, it is between Thursday and today that you remember that he was replacing somebody, standing in for somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: It is between Thursday and today that you remember that he was standing in for somebody?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, perhaps he was a shift leader. I don't know. But that night, he was the shift leader.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But if he was standing in for somebody, who could it be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please come closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness C, you're being asked to come closer to the microphone. Would you move closer to the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you were questioned in the administrative building, did somebody take notes? Did somebody keep minutes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that investigator. He was writing down something with a pen in a notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did the outcome of the interrogation determine which room people would be transferred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say exactly whether it was the outcome of the interrogation which determined that, but in the early days, those interrogated were largely moved to Room 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And in those early days, was somebody released from Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How many people were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 20, since those 20 also included my eldest brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And what was your impression, were they released after the interrogation in view of the results of this interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you exactly, but more than one half of them were rearrested and taken back to the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me something about the behaviour of those investigators and guards. What was your impression? Who was subordinate to whom; guards to investigators or investigators to guards?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not think that you can put them together.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Why do you think that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I simply think that the guards had their own superiors, and the inspectors, as likely as not, had their own superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But did guards decide who would be taken for interrogation or was it the inspectors?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inspectors. They would send out a piece of paper with the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And your brother was interrogated; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Your brother who was brought in with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how did he fare during the interrogation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was ill-treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who ill-treated him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The interrogator, Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And do you know where Zigic was incarcerated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I learned, it was somewhere behind our dormitories. There was something, a prison or something, and that's where he was, I guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Zigic came to Keraterm very often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How often?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. In the beginning -- in the early days of my detention, he was there practically around the clock, and later on, after, say, a month or so, less often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But how often did Duca come?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very often.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did he come at regular intervals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: On two or three occasions you told us people wanted to see a doctor. What did that look like? Who took those people to the doctor? Who was involved in that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it depended on the shift leader. If the shift leader provide some means of transportation, then people could go to be examined.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And how often did Kajin provide transportation for detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an exact number, but altogether --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statements you also mentioned a disinfectant was sprayed around rooms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What was that? Why? Who brought it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since about 15 or 20 days after I arrived in the camp, we all contracted lice and we were infested all over, hair and body, and we were then ordered to bring everything out of the dormitory and then the place was disinfected and we were sprayed on the hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Now, I should briefly like to go to the massacre. Who from your dormitory went out to collect the bodies, if you know their names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell us, then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already said Senad Altak, I believe his name was. He was from my dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And that morning, did you see anyone in the Keraterm compound whom you did not see regularly in the camp, that is others than guards, police officials, or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see Zivko that morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No answer]. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Let me now turn to your beating. You said that these people were wearing masks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I conclude or infer that they were probably wearing masks so that you wouldn't recognise them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if they didn't want to be recognised, that means that they were in fear that you might say this to someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can assume that that was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So they were afraid of someone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was their conscience.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In addition to their conscience, was there anything more tangible that they might have been afraid of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps that somebody would survive and then talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were afraid that the inmates whom they were taking out and perhaps survive would later on accuse them of something.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So you assumed that they already had that in mind when they were wearing masks, that they would foresee something like this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if they could have foreseen something, but this is how they behaved.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that you're the only person who says that he was beaten by masked men in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of anyone else who was beaten by masked persons, in addition to yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Who was this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seventy per cent of the inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you name one, two, five of them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are 155 names I can mention.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please name one.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say when Alisic was taken out of my room, that was -- they would call out everybody from Alisici who was in the room, and this was usually done by men who were wearing masks, but men like Ziga or Duca did not wear masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did these men wearing masks come in front of the room and call out detainees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would I be mistaken in concluding that this was, then, a frequent pattern?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On average, every third night people were called out and beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, no. I'm just asking about the masked men.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is -- these were not masks. These were hoods. People -- men were just put on hoods when they would call men out. In other words, they did not wear masks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You were talking about the months of June and July. How did they have hoods during that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: These wartime uniforms, as -- they had hoods, in other words they had -- they would put those hoods on. In other words, they were wearing this winter SMB overcoats in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I remember that on Thursday, you said that the temperature during that period reached 34, 35 Centigrade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: During one period it was terribly hot and there were showers, but throughout that period, it was terribly hot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So I assume that it was part of the military discipline that they wore -- they were wearing these winter-time hooded jackets?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The daytime and night-time temperature varied quite significantly, 10, 15 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Perhaps I could jog your memory. You said that these -- you could only see eyes and the Trial Chamber heard that. Do you still maintain that they only had hoods on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Then how would that -- how could you say that if they all were wearing hoods?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me put it this way: It was 12.00 at night, and if somebody is wearing a -- if somebody is wearing a hood, you can only see his eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What about the nose, the beard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was afraid to look. Maybe I just flashed a glance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And if the floodlights are shining, you couldn't -- couldn't you see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you couldn't. There were no floodlights at the time. They came later.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Later how?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Much later, after my arrival.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Everything that you know happened after your arrival there because -- you don't have to point that out especially. What I'm asking you is what happened during your time there? If you cannot respond, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the men in the hoods, about what was going on when they were taking you out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they took me out, there were no floodlights, so that I could not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I have only two additional questions. Can we please move into the private session again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I wasn't clear, Mr. Petrovic, are you finished with your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have finished. Thank you very much. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness C. My name is Dusan Vucicevic and I am counsel for Dragan Kolundzija. I will start first when you testified on Thursday, you were asked which shift was the better shift. You answered not in comparative, you answered in superlative. "For instance, Kole's shift was the best." Didn't you say that? I would expect from you answers basically yes or no, and if there is going to be any need to comment of anything what I say, the Trial Chamber will allow the Prosecutors to ask you additionally so that we can go quickly through this. So did you say this? It's in the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the witness being directed by my friend to answer yes or no. In my submission, he should be able to answer every question appropriately. He should not be limited to a yes or no answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll deal with the appropriateness of the witness' answers. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: This was direct quotation from the record, Witness C, so I just read it to you. So did you say that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What exactly is the question, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just asking to reaffirm whether he remembers his statement, because I want to get some answers in addition to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you say that, Witness C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible in that chaos that shift was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I move that this part of the answer be stricken as non-responsive. I just read from his testimony verbatim what he said and he is not responding to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness C, the counsel is merely reminding you of something which you said in --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: On Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: On Thursday. Was that in examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This was directly what I am reading from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, why don't you just proceed --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- if it's there in the transcript then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C, you were allowed to get out from the -- from your room in the daytime on some shifts; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And on shift, and one of the shift on which Dragan Kolundzija was a shift leader, at some time, you were allowed to spend time outside of the room all day long from 6.00 in the morning to 6.00 in the afternoon when Kolundzija was there; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you have also indicated that nobody was beaten or tortured on Kole's shift?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And there was a reputation for Kole's shift that the prisoners could sleep well at ease at night because his shift used to lock up the doors; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So that reputation wouldn't have developed if there were any beatings or torture happening at night on his shift; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part when he was present, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you did not remember in the statements that you have given to AID on June 27th of 2000 and the subsequent statement that you have given to OTP on August 30th of 2000, you have never mentioned that anybody has been beaten on the Kole's shift. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I really do appreciate and empathize with you for having gone through your life through such an ordeal but, indeed, facing this Court is an also ordeal for my client, and being a professional man that you are, I ask you to help the Court with precise answers. I ask the Court to instruct the witness to answer the previous question, not mainly because did he or didn't he make a statement to that effect that -- to the previous authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, he did say "for the most part", and that's his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So, Witness C, you don't remember whether you said in those two statements anything about Kole's shift, do you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your recollection today that when you were questioned in June and in August last year, you didn't say anything about Kole's shift, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for the night when the massacre took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me -- if we go into the private session, Your Honour, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When you were asked the question about the types of water that was available at Keraterm, you said that it was at the beginning, industrial water.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that you do not know with absolute certainty that that is industrial water, that's your -- what you've heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it only as I told you here, that it was water from the hose used to wash the WCs. And when we had our meals, there was this hydrant, and that is where we managed to quickly rinse the bowls and perhaps drink some water if we were sufficiently fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you didn't drink that water and the other people didn't drink that water. That's correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And -- the prior witnesses, that water has been -- has been used for drinking purposes. However, you have mentioned that that water has caused dysentery. Perhaps you have meant to say that that water had caused diarrhoea, something that you could observe; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Dysentery is a medical diagnosis involved medical investigation. You can't say that -- not even a doctor could say just -- strike it. Not a man cannot say any kind of a diarrhoea is a dysentery.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the consequences, and the cause I can guess it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: It was summertime. It was extremely hot. And there are so many other sources that could cause diarrhea as a symptom of an intestinal disease. That's possibility. And one of the -- what common sense implies is that one of the sources of diarrhea could be a food poisoning. I'm not saying there was plenty of food. I'm not saying the food was properly delivered. I'm just merely mentioning that is one of the possibilities.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is also possible that the WC was a cause because we had to walk out -- to step over excrement to get to the WC.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... inmates were using -- having some vessels, some containers, it was irregular supplies, there were irregular vessels, but it could be that because of the general unsanitary conditions, that came to the contamination of the water that inmates had in their own possessions. That is also a possibility.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that it was the only cause, I'm saying that's one, perhaps one of many that could have caused it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And it's a summer. There are so many types of diarrhoeas that are caused by so many bacteria and viruses, if you had heard it, because you have had high school education and those things were discussed in those days, if you do know, classical high school in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you know, say whether you know. If you don't, say so. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps those things could cause diarrhea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I suspect --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to clear up the points --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is your other hat.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't do anything medically here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement on June 27th to AID, but let me go back a little bit here. Were you describing how was that statement taken, where, who was present?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was, what shall I call it, an official of that police station or whatever, and they invited me to come and make a statement, rather they invited me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... in Bosnian to the fellow officer to AID who took it in Bosnian, there was no need to have an interpreter. That's correct. The third person was not interpreter.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: There were no -- the person was not member of the OTP or any other international organisation, so that any other language but Bosnian had to be spoken.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Was a written statement made at the end of your interview which you have signed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You signed that statement at that given time being that that statement was written in Bosnian when you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Having been elected a president, and you know what I am referring to, it was your intent at that time to give all the information that you knew to the investigators, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, only the information that he was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did, at any time throughout that interview, an officer who interviewed you, did he ask you whether you were willing to testify before this Honorable Court?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So as far as you remember today about event that happened nine months ago, you are not sure whether the question was posed to you, "Are you willing to go The Hague and testify?"

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, you had made a statement, and now because these are your words and I want to speak them verbatim, so I will read this in B/C/S. I'm citing, [Interpretation] "We then heard that one of the soldiers is saying let them break the glass and the entrance door." [In English] This statement you have also signed on 30th of August in the presence of the OTP investigators who have asked you to more or less ratify this statement as yours; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did they ask you or -- I'm sorry, did they explain you why there was a need to sign that statement again, because you had it signed before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If that is possible, do you remember today and could you tell this Honorable Court what is it they tell you on that day why your second signature was necessary? If you can't remember, you can't remember, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't -- no, it doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: However, the original didn't have the attestation clause. The original didn't have a statement where you swear to the truthfulness of your statement. Perhaps that is why the officer asked you to resign it after asking you whether the statement that you had given on June 27th is the truth, the whole truth, and that's why you co-signed a statement and put the date, the date when you signed it second time. Because as a matter of fact, that is indicated in your statement that you have made to the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But also in a statement on August 30th which was properly signed and where you have -- I just want to make sure I read from that statement where it says, and I will read it in Bosnian, [Interpretation] "This statement was read out to me in Bosnian and it contains everything that I said according to the best of my recollection and knowledge. I gave this statement of my own free will, and I am aware that it may be used in legal proceedings before the International Criminal Tribunal for the prosecution of persons responsible for serious violations of international law committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991, and that I may be called to give evidence in public before the Tribunal." This was read out to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And before that, did you go through the written statement that was made before you, did you read it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And you signed it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Which means this statement says, "... and it includes all that I said to the best of my knowledge and recollection." However, in this statement, when do you speak about the 24th of July, you say, "We heard soldiers shouting, 'Break the door. Break the windows.'" [In English] You never mentioned Kole's name in first or the second statement. That is evident from the statements?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I already said that that statement to the investigation documentation agency, that is AID, was an occult statement, that is it was done very quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, allow the witness to finish.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said all that I had to say in about 15 minutes time, and the second statement took four days, sir. So that --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: That's the point that I'm driving at, sir. Because the second statement you had given in four days, and you have not mentioned -- you do not remember that that was Kole who said that because on Thursday when you testified, you suddenly remembered it was Kole. So my question is: Who told you that was Kole who said, "Break the windows"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps it was Kole, but from that direction, we heard it from those soldiers. It could have been Kole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So your testimony from Thursday, now you are reneging on that. So it was Kole or it wasn't Kole.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: What is your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was Kole.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you think or you do know?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say it was -- I'm sure, 90 per cent that it was him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How do you conclude that 90 per cent that it was him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The sequence of events when Kole came to our dormitory to tell us, "There are soldiers outside. They cannot keep the situation under control. Don't stand up. They'll slay you all." Then he walked away some 20 metres or so from the dormitory and what prevails at that moment are those words of his. For instance, as he deploys these -- as he deploys the soldiers when he shouts "Don't shoot. Don't shoot." When he participates in the positioning of those soldiers, how they should be positioned, where, those are his words. His speech was predominated and one could distinguish it from the background noise of those other soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... about what Kole said in June and in July? You have testified about him indicating "Don't shoot. Don't stand here. Go there." But never you mentioned that was him that said, "Break the windows." And that detail is very important. Because not only did you said not "Break the windows," because you have indicated on 20 -- in June and in August, you said "Break the windows and break the doors." So what did Kole, indeed, say and who told you that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things I am repeating this. He said what you want to know. So he said, "Break the windows. Break down the door." Because presumably, there was no air in Room 3 and people were suffocating, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me just wind this up, this is an important point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, according to the time--

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have come to the time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I can have 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement on June 27 that you gave to AID, you are quoting Hodzic, Izet, who was your worker whom you recognised two days after the incident of 24th and you said what you heard from him. I'll quote in Bosnian [Interpretation] "He told me that their door was closed and people suddenly began to behave abnormally and started shoving, pushing and beating the detainees -- the detainees began shoving and pushing and fighting. [In English] Did you hear that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite so, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And also you testified earlier and said that were some Serbian songs there.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You also have heard that there was -- from one of your statements, and please forgive me that I can't quote it, but I'm going to quote the word that stuck in my mind, you said [Interpretation] "Noise was heard from Room 3," to one of the investigators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Singing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So there was -- to say that mildly, there was a chaos in that room at that time. I'm not trying to assign the responsibility to anything, I'm just saying what you could hear. At that time it seems there was a chaos for whatever reason. That would be fair to say.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll say what we in Room 1 heard that singing -- was that singing, and after that, later on, from the statement of this witness whom you mentioned, my co-worker, and other detainees who survived Room 3, they claimed that something had been thrown in, some poison or something, and Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 after that, they lost control over themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: This would be a good time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: May I ask how much longer will your cross-examination be?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: One more hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: One hour, I see. Yes. Well, we will take the break. And you are reminded, Witness C, not to discuss your evidence with anybody, including members of the Prosecution team. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic? You had given us an estimate of one more hour to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: A bit less than an hour. I went over my notes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. We would like you to try to conclude in a shorter time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it should be shorter than an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C, you have testified that on or about July 11th, you were taken out, and just before the beating was to take place, a truck came into the gate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let me follow it up. You have said that there was a man by the name Tomo that came up at that time. You said it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the second time I was called out.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: We are in agreement on that one. Could you describe that man?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen him that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How far away from you was he when he yelled and cursed the soldiers so they ran away? How far away from you was he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, he arrived in a van, and this van went along the tarmac moving in the direction of Room 1, and shown us who were in Room 1 -- I was in front of it and I was inside, and the guards were outside, but so they were about 30, 40 metres away and I could hear it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You are saying that he was like halfway on pista between the weigh bridge and Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Were any other prisoners outside who were beaten at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My brother and I were called out first.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that Tomo was chief, or shift leader?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that the next day because I was interested in it. It turned out that this man, by appearing, saved my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Who told you that that was Tomo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inmates who probably knew him, or who may have known the guards who were able to say who it was that actually arrived at that time, who it exactly was.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to remind you, because you said in your statement that was given in August of 2000, and also you testified on Thursday in court, that you were accompanied by Witness A at that time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me try to explain it. Because it took about 15 minutes for this calling out of my brother and myself to take place, and I, as I said, I told them that I was in number 4, then they went over to check that at the reception office. But the practice was, when an inmate refused to respond, then the room leader would be called upon to find him and, if that didn't help, then they would take the first ten, 15 inmates.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] if you remember, wasn't that Witness A who knew all the guards, was it perhaps him who told you that was Tomo, at that moment, because he could have recognised him, that him having been a shift leader, either by sight or by voice? If you remember, was it Witness A who told you that, right at that moment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was under obligation to bring me over here, but I don't know whether he said that or whether the next day I heard it from someone else, either an inmate or a guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So since that was --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: For me, it did not matter very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I neglected to say that I had been asked by the interpreters to let you know that you are not observing the pause between question and answer, and that creates difficulties for the interpreters. Witness C, the same applies to you, particularly since you both speak the same language. The temptation is to move very quickly but bear in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would apologise on behalf of both participants in this colloquy. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But one thing that we can agree for sure that it wasn't Kole's shift because it was Tomo's. That is correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Have you ever inquired either at that time or later when was Tomo shift leader, in what period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So is your testimony that Tomo was coming on and off as a shift leader or he was there for a certain period of time and then didn't appear anymore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's say the latter version. In my view, he was there for a very brief period of time, not frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So he was there for a week or two after you were arrested and then he stopped coming; isn't that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly whether it was one week or two weeks after my arrival there, but I remember him very well on that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... coming regularly as a shift leader. Is that your conclusion?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No that's not what I said, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... could you help us out --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very infrequently. For instance, I heard about him that night and I may have seen him another couple of times or three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a Defence exhibit that I would like the usher to distribute. Your Honours, those are the copies of the originals, or at least they purport to be the originals here which I'd like the usher to put on ELMO and perhaps, you know, to give them to you after I address the witness so you can view the original because those are the best copies that we could get being that this is an old document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, some of them are barely legible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, that's why you will have an opportunity to view the originals. Couldn't do any better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is this anyway? What is this supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a daily schedule of personnel of police station Prijedor number 2 for June 5th, 1992 and for June 6th, 1992. And if you would respectfully turn to the last page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of which one?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Of both of them, if you look at the last page. You will see on the top, there is Roman three and underneath in the first column to the left there is security Keraterm 07 to 07. And the other one has the same markings on the page 3. And on the original, I am not quite sure whether you can see, there is a signature on the bottom of the page and says commandeer, that means commanding officer, Knezevic, Zivko. And I would like to show that to the witness being that he is familiar with the record-keeping procedures in his background, he can testify about this document. It is going to conclusively shed some light on how many shifts on those two days. I was fortunate to find these originals, and I would like to present it to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, although the document is by and large a listing with names, there are other parts of it which should be translated for us to make sense of it. For example, what are the headings? They are not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in due course I will tender the translation of those documents, but for the purpose of getting information and testimony of this witness, he can read those headings and they will be translated to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Go ahead, and let's see how far we can get with it. Go ahead, Mr. Vucicevic. The witness has the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just like to give a minute or two for the witness to look over the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C, I would like to kindly direct your attention at the page number 3 of those documents. Could you take a look at the headlines and also could you take a look at the signature at the bottom and the signature itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, he has seen them. What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you move that document further down on the ELMO so we can see the top of the document? Could you put the first page of that document on the ELMO, please? Mr. Usher, could you put the originals on the ELMO, because we can't see anything from there. That's why I gave you the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C, could you please read what is being -- what is written on that first heading?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the duty service --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- work schedule, and then something really illegible, RSM or something, Prijedor, Roman numeral 2 for 6 June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And looking at that document, the original, is that the type of a paper that was used in 1992 in the administrative services in Prijedor? Was that type of paper used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you show us the last page of the same document, Mr. Usher? On the left-hand side it says obisbedzena Keraterm from 07 to 07; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Obisbedzena means Keraterm, by the way.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] the names that you see in the left-hand column?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Tomo Prodan, Ignjatije Lajic, Zoran Grahovic, Lazo Gavrilovic, Goran Koralija, Slavisa Davidovic, Drasko Sobot, Mladen Radisid, Miroslav Vujicid, Miljan Sanovic, Zoran Zigic, Nebojsa Banovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] part of the column, there is another column of names which reads Slobodni, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Slobodni" means off duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you read those names?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Damir Dosen, Drasko Dosen, Mladen Madjar, Drasko Bucalo, Predrag Cicic, Mladen Pilipovic, Drasko Jeric, Dragan Kolundzija, Dragan Zurnic, Radomir Radakovic, Drasko Stakic. And sick leave and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please show us the signature on the same page? Sir, could you please read what is being typed there in that signature section?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What it states is, "Commanding Officer Zivko Knezevic."

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] seem to have been written in ink on that original?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it looks like.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Let's assume now that this document was, as it purports to be, a schedule of -- a daily schedule of the police station number 2, signed by the commander Knezevic Zivko. Does it recall -- does it now jog your memory that at the beginning there were only two shifts, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So does it mean that on that day, on 6th of June, there were two shifts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He said no.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: How would I know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: He has already said no, so I don't think it's proper to follow up with a question which assumes that he answered otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do apologise, but I might have not heard correctly. I asked at that time and then the following question was on that day, but that's -- if you would permit me to ask him specifically for this given day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document speaks for itself and I object to this witness being asked questions about the meaning of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What's your specific question?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: That document indicates that there were two shifts on the given day, and to ask the witness, does he agree that at the beginning there were two shifts working from 7.00 a.m. to 7.00 a.m. the other day, 24 hour a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But I've already indicated I think your premise is wrong because the witness has already answered that to him the document does not indicate that there were two shifts. So I'm going to disallow the question. Move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you pull down the document so I can see those?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When you read the first line on the left-hand side, Witness C, doesn't it say security detail Keraterm 07 to 07?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: In your previous testimony you have testified that at the beginning there were three shifts that worked from 7.00 to 15 hours then from 15 to 21 or 22 and then another one from 22 to -- does this document in any way change your testimony that, at the beginning, there were two shifts that worked 24 hours and not three shifts that worked eight hours apart?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you in a position to answer that question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do believe that three shifts existed, as I stated previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, this is a document which no doubt may be of use to your case. When you come to present your case, you will be in a position to call witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am just merely using this document to refresh the witness' memory, and if I may have another question, because the witness has testified that Mr. Tomo Prodan was a shift commander and -- strike it -- shift leader. And here it seems that there is a name of Tomo Prodan with the names of the other people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have an objection from Ms. Baly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to the question on the basis that it can't possibly assist the witness' recollection given that the witness wasn't arrested until the 12th of June. So when he refers to "the beginning", it's a different time frame. This document is dated the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are in agreement with Ms. Baly. I think the proper course for you is to produce this document in your case. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please collect these documents, and if I could have back the originals.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C, you have testified that there were three shifts in the collection centre, as you called it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Was Tomo one of the commanders at the time when you arrived to the collection centre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So it is your testimony that Tomo was named or appointed a shift leader at some time after you were confined?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. I only know how many times I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether Tomo worked as the shift leader any time while there were three shifts which worked 8 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not. Not in the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So when was it that the timing of the shifts were changed from 8 hours to 12 hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. How could I know?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: At the time that you were beaten, were they two shifts or three shifts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will proceed with the -- when you were taken out and beaten for the first time, how many men were beating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe there were five of them, but how many of them beat me, I don't know because I faced the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: His Honour Judge Robinson asked you what they were beating you with, you answered with a police baton. How many batons were there that you were beaten with?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose not many, perhaps one or two, and also their army boots.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... would you tell us on what part of the body they were hitting you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the back and kidney area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did they hit you a single time over your head?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: If you received 50 blows with that baton over your head, do you think you would have survived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, no. At that time I was already a seasoned inmate, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But perhaps you didn't receive that many over your back. You received less than 50 blows over your back, did you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they counted traces afterwards, because there were signs, Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 there were bruises, 20, 30 times, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But I'm particularly interested about these blows over the head. If you, for example, received five blows over the back of your head, do you think you would have survived it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Baly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: The witness cannot possibly answer that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think you should proceed to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Have you seen anybody hit with a police baton over his head, and I ask you: Have you seen?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, perhaps, for instance, when we would go to have lunch and they made us hurry. On such occasions one could hear blows on the head or back. One could see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the man who was hit over his head with the police baton?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already explained that. It depended on how long that man had been in the camp. If he was new, then he still had enough strength and then he would have survived. If he had spent some time in the camp, then his strength would have already been sapped, and I suppose he would have fallen down. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... the power takeover in municipality of Prijedor on 30th of April, however, in your statement, you have -- that you have given to the OTP on August 30th of 2000, you said, "In March and April," I am going to cite your exact words in Bosnian [Interpretation] "In March and April I did not come to work regularly." [Previous translation continues] [In English] ... power takeover before the checkpoints were set, why you didn't go to work in March and April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because as early as the beginning of the year, as I have already said, beginning of 1992, there was this unwritten rule that Muslims and Croats who did not put on the military uniform, which I suppose was to mean a tacit sign -- indication of loyalty, that such people could not come to the compound of the company.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... by Mr. Petrovic earlier today you said that nobody was allowed to come to work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... didn't have them yourselves. Those are your exact words; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the counsel please not speak at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic and Witness C, the interpreters are asking you not to speak at the same time. Please observe the pause.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Witness C, I'm going to read now from the statement of a gentleman who was incarcerated at Keraterm at first, and later in Omarska. And in the same kind of a sworn statement that you have given on 23rd of September of 1994, he had said the following: "On 22nd of May I travelled to my work at Celpak by bus as usual at 6.00. Everything seemed to be normal, although it was not very easy to travel by bus. There were not many buses running on schedule, and I had to cross three Serb checkpoints from the entrance from my village to Prijedor. There were also guards at the entrance to Celpak. On 22nd of May I was the only one to show up at my work centre. I expected two other colleagues, one Muslim and one Serb, who failed to show up. I learned the Serb went to the front line in Bosnia, and I don't know what happened to the Muslim. I could not do anything of my own, but I stayed at work. No trains came to Celpak that day so at about 1800, I departed work to the bus stop to catch the 1900 bus to Ljubija." So isn't it true that at least one man travelled, a Muslim from a village outside of Prijedor, who was daily catching a train or a bus, managed to go every day to his post. We can agree on that, could we?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. All I do know, since it is a different company, I know how things were in my company in the iron ore mine where my brothers worked and very many relatives, some 50 relations of mine worked there, and could not go to work just as I couldn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So you testified earlier you were only referring to your firm but not on all firms in Prijedor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak about my company, of course, and as for the others, from conversations with relatives, with friends, from what we could hear, I heard from them that they could not go. But there are always exceptions, you know. There are 3.000 workers and one manages to go; it's quite possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: This man indeed said in a sworn statement, there was two of them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, but let me explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I only asked you whether he said whether there was another one besides him, in this statement that we just read. Well, you said earlier that your position was -- had a good measure of a political position, because it required membership in a party to obtain that position; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: But it was a management position, you were not a -- wasn't it? That we can agree on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your answer. Was it management position or not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was. Persons with special powers, that is with special authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You testified that you were losing the confidence of your authorities in May and April because you also said that you were officially dismissed after the power takeover.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1991 and in early 1992, 99 per cent of the Muslim and Croat population did not go to work. Whether they were -- tacitly had a paid leave or a non-paid leave, but be that as it may, nobody called us to go to work, and we were made to understand that we were not to come to work unless we wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
