utterances.text: Let me see whether we can understand that in the context of mobilisation that had happened in Prijedor area. Was there a mobilisation of all military-able men in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the front in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Majority of military-able men who opposed -- who opposed military solution in Croatia refused to respond to the call-up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what was the percentage of the Prijedor military-able men that refused the call-up? Isn't it fair to say that most of the men who refused were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question or --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I will read back this question from the transcript. Could you tell the Court what was the percentage of the Prijedor militarily-able men that refused the call-up? Isn't it fair to say that the most of men who refused were of non-Serb ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could say so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: The Prijedor had a vibrant economy before the war, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And in order to sustain a war effort, a workforce is needed for any economy, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's take it that it is so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So one would expect that men who do not wish to put on their military uniform would be gainfully and usefully employed in the economy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's a comment, Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: I'll take it back, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You said that situation was different in March and April. Does that mean that Serb soldiers that came back from Croatia took up their position in the economy so they were not needed in the military anymore?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. Nobody gave a thought to business at the time. All they thought about was war.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: There was a war indeed in Croatia at that time, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to any Serb to ask them what war did they think about? Because you just testified they were thinking about the war.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I think that the war had already started in Bosnia at that time. I don't remember exactly but I think that in March, in April, things were already stirring.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues].

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ravno? Ravno is in Bosnia, I suppose, somewhere in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned about military activities had started and they started in March, so I would appreciate if you could place that location a little bit more with precision for the court to follow.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean, the location?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us is it close to Ravno? On what road is it located? Is it close to any borders with any other republics?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: And the --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose it is near the border with Croatia down in the south.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] work because there was feeling that the war might erupt, and the first -- you just described the first activity and it seems you don't know anything about it. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: How can I know what went on in Croatia, and other towns? I know about Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vucicevic, I think you have now exceeded the time limit which you yourself had set. Could you bring the cross-examination to a close, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: This is a picture of the view at Keraterm building with the rooms 1 and 2 in forefront, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is, and Room 3 I think you can see also.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues], isn't it? Okay. Could you indicate with the marker there where was Dragan Kolundzija when you heard him speaking those words that you already testified about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, what words do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: When he came up and when he talked to you at first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, well, that was -- that was in the doorway, and the door of the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] the very door of your Room number 1? How long did he stay there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then very briefly just to tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How many times during that night did you see in front of the door of Room 1?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of the door when this was all that he told us. I saw him only once at the door, except that later on I heard his voice when he was some 15 metres away from the entrance into the dormitory.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... recognition of his voice that you testify about interest those that you have seen him in front of the door or those that he was about 15 metres away; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he moved about in front of the dormitory. Sometimes he would draw nearer, sometimes he would go further away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: How far back was he going? You said you've seen him at 15 metres, was he going 20, 25, 30?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but always close enough so that we could hear him.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: You testified that he was quarreling with soldiers and that he told them, "Not here. There," to that effect. Those were his words.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So isn't it true that the soldiers that he was talking to, those were soldiers that were behind his back. Where he was standing here, 15, 20, 30 metres on the pista, there were the soldiers that could hear him that were behind his back?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say behind his back or rather to the side because they were taking up positions in the semicircle or perhaps they were on the level with him because they all moved around.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... you testified about it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: So if you heard it, Kolundzija must have heard clicking of those arms behind his back too; that's fair to say?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vucicevic. Any re-examination, Ms. Baly?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Just for the record, Witness C, the last series of questions that you were referred to by Mr. Vucicevic referred to the Room 3 massacre; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You've referred in your evidence to a person by the name of Tomo who you said was a shift leader who appeared infrequently in the camp. Do you know the full name of the person Tomo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I saw on this list what it is, but I had not known it. I only know that he was the shift leader on the night when I was called out, and as for the rest, I saw him very infrequently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were asked some questions by Mr. Vucicevic regarding Kole's shift and the effect of your answers was for the most part that beatings did not take place on Kole's shift. Can you explain, please, what you meant by the phrase "for the most part"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I did not know Kole at that time, I could not pay special attention to that shift. However, it could happen that when Kole was not around, that the guards would call someone out without his knowledge, and do some harm in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness C, you were asked a number of questions regarding the searchlights and, in particular, when they were placed in the position that you've drawn them on the sketch. You said that was some 20 days before the camp closed. My question is: Were the searchlights placed there before or after the Room 3 massacre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before, before. In retrospect I think that that was the only reason why they were placed there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic asked you some questions and you referred to persons by the name of Banovic or the Banovics. Who were they?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew them by sight from the town. They were nice guys. Unfortunately in Keraterm they were terrible, especially the one whom we called Cupo. He was quite a bloodthirsty one.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How many Banovics were there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two, and I think that they were twins. The ones that I knew.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You referred to one as Cupo, do you know the full name of that person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nenad, I think, or something like that, but his nickname was Cupo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And how, Witness C, did Cupo behave in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of whether it was day or night, he would call out camp inmates and ask for money. He exclusively asked for money. He would give us a deadline, say 10 minutes to collect, I don't know, a certain amount of money, or he would put -- he could designate a person who would collect the money, and if the money was not collected, we would suffer. Either the person who was tasked with it or he would come into the room. For instance, if we were -- if there was a lunch to be served, he would give us a minute for 30 of us to finish lunch. And within a minute, they can barely ladle out the meal, and we had to go back. I know on one occasion I happened to pass by on the way to the toilet when he ordered an inmate to find him 100 marks. He did not manage to find it, and he ordered him to put his hand against the wall and he broke his lower arm with the baseball bat.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: On whose shift did he work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was in Kajin's shift.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And you have referred to another person who was his twin. Do you know what his full name was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but the other brother was much, much better, at least from my point of view. I think he was much better. I think that during the day he did not take such a lead in these things as the other one, from what I could observe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: How were you able to distinguish the two brothers from each other?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The very nickname, I think, describes it. One had a shorter hair and was more solid, if I can put it that way. In other words, he was not very aggressive.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Which one was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one with the longer hair whom we called Cupo. He was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: You were asked some questions about the water that you've labelled "industrial water" that the inmates drank. Did that water have any particular taste?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell you. At that moment we just needed to drink any water, regardless of what it smelled or tasted like. If you did not take water for two or three days, any water is sweet. We were eager to have any kind of water to drink.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: And finally, Witness C, it was put to you by Mr. Greaves that life continued as normal after the takeover, and you said, "No, no, it was normal for Serb people but not for others." Firstly, who do you mean by "others"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, along with my brothers, I had to sign off on a paper declaring that I was leaving all of my property behind because in the camp, and after the camp, they were trying to convince us that we could no longer live there together.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, objection. The answer is not responsive. The question was what had happened after the takeover. The witness is talking what happened after he was released from the camp. Three months' difference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you answer the question more specifically, Witness C?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify it for me?

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Witness, the answer you gave was in response to a question by Mr. Greaves that life continued as normal after the takeover of Prijedor and you said, "No, no. It was normal for Serb people but not for others." The question I asked is, who do you mean by "others"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Specifically, I think you mean what ethnic groups are comprised in the "others"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, that is clear. That would have meant for Croats and Muslims there was hell, and for the Serbs life continued as they chose it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Apart from the situation with employment which you've already described, how exactly was life not normal, or hell, as you've described Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS C:  [Resumed]
utterances.text: Listen, when -- after the camp, I expected them to come for me every night. In other words, I did not dare sleep in my own house at that time. I slept in the garage. The overall situation -- the overall attitude towards the non-Serb population was such that any uniformed soldier could knock on my door, take us out, mistreat us, rob us, and in the end, kill us, without any liability. The life of non-Serb population was worth nothing.

utterances.speaker: MS. BALY
utterances.text: Those are my questions, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Baly. Witness C, that concludes your evidence and you are released. We will take the adjournment now, until 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, you are going to take the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. And just for the record and to refresh the Bench's memory, this is one of the witnesses who was previously granted both protective measures, a pseudonym and facial distortion, in the December 22nd, 2000 order of the Chamber. So we simply just need to re-designate the pseudonym under which he was allowed to testify, but he is one of the ones already granted the facial distortion measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And also while the usher is retrieving the witness, I would ask that the first four or five questions, I would respectfully request that we go into private session for those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Pseudonym for the next witness will be Witness D.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness comes in, I would object to the part of the testimony of this witness when he is transferred to Omarska and whatever happened while he was at Omarska, because we have in his proffer here from paragraph 30 thereon, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: From paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 30 and everything from paragraph 31 until the end I object to. First 30 paragraphs, I have no objection to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No doubt you can make that point. I said you can make that point when we get to that. Are you objecting to the evidence being led at all or are you objecting to counsel leading the witness in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: No. I object to any evidence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any evidence at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: -- entering what had happened when he was transferred to Omarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You can make that point when we reach there. Yes, let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, we are currently in private session which means that the questions that I'm going to ask will not --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are still in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Do you want to go in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the first few questions, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we are now in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, did you do compulsory service in the JNA and if so, can you please tell us the years and places where you served?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. In 1983-84, first in Ljubijana and then in Sordorica [phoen] in the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, prior to the war, immediately prior to the war, what was your employment?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I worked for the central workshop of the iron ore mine in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you a member of the SDA and, if so, how actively did you participate in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you actively participate as a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, would you characterise your family as being one that was particularly religious and, if so, what religion did your family practice?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We are Muslims. We are believers. We had no brush with the law. No one of us has a criminal record. We've never caused any trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would like to draw your attention to early 1992. Did there come a time that you joined the police reserve in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, or rather in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For the record, can you tell us how far Ljubija is from the town of Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: 10 maybe 11 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the circumstances surrounding your joining the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Active policeman, Rade Zekan, came to my place one day and asked me, because they were short of staff in the police station and that I had not a criminal record and my conduct was exemplary, and he asked me if I wanted to join them. And if yes, then I should report to the chief of the police station in Ljubija and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what date you were approached to join the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Towards the very end of [redacted]1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were you issued any special type of equipment once you joined the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When I reported to the chief of the police station in Ljubija, after a short interview, I was issued with an automatic rifle and 150 bullets and sent to Prijedor to get my uniform, and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What type of special training, if any, did you receive as part of the being a member of the reserve police force?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I had no training apart from repeating exercises concerning the manipulation of the automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And was this training just more or less a follow on to the type of training you had received in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. That's right. We more or less repeated the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, can you briefly describe the relationship between the reserve police force and the active police force in opstina Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, those were all normal circumstances. Before the war we came from all sides, from all ethnic groups. At that time, at the time when I joined the reserve police force, the relations were, let me say, normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall specifically the date or time frame when the war, as you put it, came to Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The proper war, or rather the beginning of the war, perhaps I could say it was the time of the takeover of power in Prijedor, and that was in late April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, what was your first date as a reserve police officer in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The [redacted], afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that was the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [redacted].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did he, in fact, arrive at your house that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the two of you then go somewhere together? And if so, where?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. He came and said that Serbs, his fellow workers, sometime after midnight, had pointed their weapons at him and said to him, "Sorry, you have to go home. Serbs are now taking over the power, and only Serbs can stay on in the police." Then we went together to the police station in Ljubija and there we talked with people who told us -- or rather the chief there, who told us that he did not have any instructions as to what we were to do, that we should go home and to behave as previously agreed, which meant that I was to take on my shift when it was due except that [redacted] and other policemen who had arrived and who had been removed from work in a similar way were assigned to the police station in Ljubija until further notice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned other policemen. Was there -- how many other policemen were in the same situation that you mentioned, that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: [redacted] know his first name, can't remember it. And there were [redacted] more, I believe, that came from Brdo, whom I did not know before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I believe you mentioned [redacted]. Do you know that person's first name and that person's ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, [redacted], a Croat from the neighbouring locality of Kaljevo [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And after you had this conversation, did you then return home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time either that day or shortly thereafter that a group, a large group of refugees began arriving in Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please describe the circumstances surrounding the arrival of these refugees, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Those were the days in early May and from the neighbourhood municipality, Bosanski Novi, from the village of Agici, refugees began to arrive, first in small groups, and warned us that a column of refugees was on the way and that they would arrive during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you first saw these refugees, where were you and what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I was on a regular shift at the railway station checkpoint, and I saw a column of cars with white towels on them, and at first I thought that was a wedding party. And I recognised some people in those cars, and they told me that they had been attacked, that they had to leave their homes, and that they wanted to get through to their families in Prijedor. I called the chief of the police station, Byekic, and he escorted them on towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you indicated that you were on a regular shift. Was that a regular shift as a reserve police officer on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in relation to Ljubija, can you briefly tell the Court where Bosanski Novi is located and specifically the village of Agici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Well, depends which direction you take. If you take the normal road from Prijedor to Bosanski Novi, then before Bosanski Novi, a few kilometres before it, across the river Japra, there is a road which leads to Agici, and if you look from Ljubija across Miska Glava, Sulko [phoen] Miska Glava, there is another road to the same village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many refugees you saw on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I cannot give you the exact number. I know there were very many. Some were in cars, some in tractors, some horse-carts and the next day, two more buses arrived. There weren't very many of them, but I wouldn't know how many exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did some of these refugees temporarily stay in the Ljubija area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many stayed in Ljubija and where did they physically stay when they were in the village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Some were accommodated in houses with their relations and also, many other people took them in even if they did not know them before, and a group was also put up in the elementary school in Ljubija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did some of these refugees stay in your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to turn your attention to the village and area of Hambarine. In relation to Ljubija, how far is it from Ljubija to Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Six, maybe seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when, to your knowledge, an ultimatum was issued to the residents of Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I did not hear the ultimatum personally. I heard about it from others. And what I know in relation to Hambarine is that while I was on duty with [redacted]I heard on the radio the conversation roughly which ran roughly like this: "We will meet in front of the old hotel, we are going to Ljubija to reconnoitre the situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, Witness, when you refer to being on duty and hearing things on the radio, would that be during the course of your serving as a reserve police officer and was the radio that you referred to the police radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate date when you heard this coming in on the radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened after you heard this information coming over the police radio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: A short while after that, one could hear -- I don't know what to call it -- one could hear cries for help on the radio station. "There is gunfire below Hambarine. There are some wounded. Please send an ambulance."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you hear any sounds that sounded like any -- like a military conflict of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Not then, but a few hours later, one could hear four detonations from the direction of Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you do after you heard these detonations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I reported to the Donja Ljubija Crisis Staff. Before that I called the police station, but nobody answered so I told them what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what did you do after you made these reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I stayed there until the end of my shift. A car then came and took us to the neighbouring checkpoint which is up to a kilometre away, and I stayed there for a while. Naturally, another shift took over from me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know if an ultimatum of any kind was issued to the residents of Hambarine and, if so, what were the terms of the ultimatum?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When I got to that other checkpoint, after quite a long while, a few hours later, Bjekic, the chief of the police came and told me to go to the school, that the school was full of refugees, and that I should stay there until they calmed down. And I went to the school. The school was full of women and children of young and old from the area of Hambarine and even from Donja Ljubija. Those houses which are nearer to Hambarine, and they told me what had happened below Hambarine and how they had been issued with the ultimatum that by noon the next day, they should deliver the policemen, Aziz, and some others. I can't recall their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the ultimatum also dealt with weapons of any kind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, weapons too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you remember happening the following day in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The next day at 12.00 sharp, the fire brigade centre in Donja Ljubija sounded a siren and shortly after that, the shelling started. It went on for quite some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall where the shells were being directed, that is, where were the shells hitting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I could not see that, I could only hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what exactly do you recall hearing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Detonations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: For approximately how long did these detonations occur?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: A long time. Well into the night, perhaps even longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall immediately before the war approximately how many people lived in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After the shelling stopped, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe -- around the same time, can you describe the situation in the Gornja Ljubija police station, what was happening there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. One evening or rather late afternoon, a car came to take us, the reserve strength of Donja Ljubija, to take us to the police station for a briefing. When we arrived there, we found there policemen from other areas of Ljubija, of course, and deputy chief of the police station, the commissar, an active-duty policeman, Bentic, and they requested a few minutes to have a good cry. Then they told us that the time had come for us to part our ways, because Muslims and Croats could not stay in the station, that Serbs were taking over the station, and he, the commissar, as an honest Serb, would stay there to try to prevent extremist Serbs from becoming members of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was the commissar successful in his attempt?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. We did not want to leave the station. We repeated that we are the people's police, that the people wanted us, and even the Serbs did not agree with that. So we requested weapons which did not exist, because Pero said that it had been taken away. And we agreed that we would stay together until the next meeting; Serbs, and Muslims, and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this meeting were you required to turn in your police-issued weapon and ammunition?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, but we had not taken our weapons along with us. Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25 Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when the active-duty police or the Serb reserve police then went to your house to collect the weapons and your uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: No. This happened later. That night, the meeting that had been arranged at night took place several days later. Meanwhile, some other things happened, the weapons were turned over to the Territorial Defence and Baja Bjekic arrived. He had been absent for some time. That is, he could not arrive in Ljubija from Prijedor via Hambarine. The reserve police officers from Ljubija and Crkolac [phoen], the Croat and Muslim police officers, that is, were assigned to duties in Ljubija. And one morning we were called into the Ljubija police station where we were met by the commander and some Serbs who were unknown to us. And in this meeting, he addressed us with the following words, he said, "As of today, this station will become Serb," that is the police will. "Some of you will not be able to stay on here." The man who was standing next to him handed him a list on which five names were listed including myself, two active duty police officers, and two from the regular roster. We immediately had to turn in our weapons. Meanwhile, by the time I had reached home, they apparently -- they arrived and they waited for me to get undressed, took the uniform and left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Of the five names that were read out that day, all of those police officers were discharged from their official duties as police officers on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What were the ethnicities of the five that were discharged?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, at about the same time, do you recall the day that you were discharged from the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: In early June.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, in the time frame of late May, early June, 1992, were you aware of other villages in the area of Prijedor town or in the opstina that were also under attack?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I know about Kozarac. Before Kozarac, the population of Crkvica were driven out, mostly Croats. I don't know about any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear an announcement on Radio Prijedor about weapons being held by civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: This kept repeating itself. Anything that was military from socks up to the weapons that were legal -- even the hunting weapons that were in possession of the Croats and Muslims had to be turned over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What about weapons that were in the hands of the Serbs? Do you know anything about those weapons? I mean Serb civilians.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I don't know. They did not turn it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: They were permitted to keep their weapons then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear any other announcements on Radio Prijedor with respect to white flags?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. All Muslims and Croats loyal to the Serb authorities were to hoist or hang out a white cloth outside their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did there come a time when your village, Donje Ljubija -- when the Serbs came to your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. That is Serbs were already there. It depends on which ones you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'm referring to groups of Serb soldiers, outside Serb soldiers, coming into the village.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. In early June, in the morning, we could hear individual shots. I stepped outside and I saw several Serbs on a hill above my house. They told me that I should tell the women to take off gold jewellery that they had and to hide the money. Meanwhile, they came down to my house. They told me to go inside the house and made it look as if the house was -- had been ransacked, and they moved on. Meanwhile, the others arrived -- started arriving. Some of them I knew, some I didn't. They asked for my personal documents and also the same of my father, and from a refugee who was staying in my house, and they all directed us to go to a meeting point where a larger group of people was. From there, they escorted us in a column to a stadium in Ljubija, and after longer period of time, they separated out certain people and they released the rest of us to our homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me just go back, Witness. I have a couple of questions with respect to when you were on your way to the stadium. Were you transported in any way or did you walk or how did you get from your house to the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: First from my home, I went to the meeting point, which was to the left, and when a larger group was formed there, they formed a column on the -- it was flanked by these armed men. And on foot they escorted us to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did anything unusual happen while you were being escorted by these soldiers that were on your flanks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Many things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Some of them were going from house to house. Many of them were driving cars belonging to people whom I knew well. And while I was walking to that meeting point along with my father, an APC tried to run us over, which we avoided by taking cover in a yard. I saw a number of people I knew, Serbs who were saying, "What is going on here?" Why were they gathering us? Why were they taking us? And things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you mentioned an APC. I assume that's an armoured personnel carrier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see any other type of military vehicles that day in your village?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, trucks and a type of jeep vehicle that the Yugoslav army had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vucicevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Objection to the translation. The first time the witness testified, he said, I believe, "military truck" not "APC." He was translated "APC." And then the second way added, he said it was APC. It was leading by Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, now, you've indicated -- you testified that after you were taken to the stadium, you were released. Can you describe for us a little bit what was happening in the stadium while you were still there, before you went home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: At the stadium the gates were closed. People whom I did not know were coming in, going out, cursing. Then Rade Bilbija came, who was being addressed by others as Vojvoda, and he said that we would be released, that only some would be kept, that we should form a column and, again, we were flanked by some -- by men, some of whom were in police, some of whom were in military uniforms. They were checking ID cards, and separated out some, and took them to the premises of the soccer club. The others who had been checked would be released through the gates and allowed to go back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you used the term Vojvoda, can you describe briefly what that term means?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I wouldn't be able to tell exactly. I had heard about Chetniks in school, some Vojvodas, and when the war started, Rade Bilbija was given this title. That is, I heard him address him in this manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many people were in the stadium that day in Gornje Ljubija?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Several hundred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know approximately how many of them were allowed to go home that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: I know that 20 to 30 were kept behind and the rest of them were released. Those who were detained were for the most part men from Hambarine and Agici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the people that were kept there that day, that were not allowed to go home from Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And of the roughly 20 to 30 people that were kept behind that day, did you ever see any of those people again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Some at Keraterm, some at Omarska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did the ones that you later met at Keraterm or Omarska tell you anything about the others that were detained and kept that day in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, that they were -- those who were from the municipality and were in Keraterm were transferred to Bosanski Novi, but that one of those who had -- was killed at Keraterm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After you were released from the stadium and you were told that you could go home, did you in fact, go home that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe what you saw when you got home on that day, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: While I was on my way home, I saw abandoned vehicles, things scattered alongside the road, like brief cases. When I arrived home, my wife told me that our neighbour had been raped, a man called [redacted] killed, and several people disappeared.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you hear anything about any kind of looting that had occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: When I arrived home, I went to my sister, along with my wife, and on our way we saw that all window shops, both private and state-owned, were -- had been smashed. From some people I learned that they had been robbed. Some had to give money because they had been threatened with having their children killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness D, did there come a time when you were once again arrested or detained by the authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the date and time that that happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: On 18 June, in the evening hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what exactly happened on that day in the evening hours?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Savo Pusac came with several other policemen. I knew their nicknames, and they said that I had to go to the police station to give a statement. They placed me in a van called Puska [phoen], who used to be the property of the Ljubija mine, and -- mining company, and they took me to the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And what happened that evening at the police station?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: There I found active duty police officers, Rade Zekan, Drincic and Daljicic, and after several pro forma questions, they told me to go to the hallway and take a seat and wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long were you at the police station on that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Three to four hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And then you were allowed to go home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. Bjekic, the police commander, arrived. And the reserve police officers, the Serbs who were new reserve police officers, one of them who knew me, said what I was doing there? Then he went upstairs, came down, and said that I could go home. I asked him if he could give me a lift? He said that he didn't have fuel but that I was free to go, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What happened the following morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Early in the morning, at 5.00, the same Savo Pusac and those who had been with him, came for me, took me to the Ljubija station, and another three men came in, were put in a vehicle, that is, and we were all taken to Keraterm camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the names of the other individuals that were in the van with you that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. They included Senad from Majdan, Fejzo, who had a pastry shop in Ljubija, and a young man whom I did not know who had a pastry shop in Prijedor which was called Zvejezdas, and he was also an ethnic Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us what happened to you when you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: We got out of the van. Some soldiers, policemen started yelling at us. They ordered us to raise our hands and to lean against a kiosk which was there to take out everything we had in our pockets. One of them started beating me on the legs, telling me to spread them wider, and after they had taken down our names, they told us to pick -- that we should pick each our own apartment, suite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What did the guards mean by pick your own suite?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: They were probably referring to the rooms where the others were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you see other people, other detainees that you knew or recognised upon your first arrival in the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes, many.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe the physical appearance of some of these individuals that you saw there that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: The image was horrifying. They were unshaven. They were burned by sun, filthy, some were beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you recall the day, the date that you arrived at Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And did you, in fact, select a room to stay in upon your arrival at Keraterm and, if so, which room?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes. I went to Room 1. I met some acquaintances there. One of them who saw me, he raised his head. He looked at me and he said that there were already two reasons for me to be killed. One was that I had a leather jacket on, and second was my appearance, that is, my height. And because everything was crowded, I tried to see whether there was any room in other rooms. In front of Room 4, I recognised Drago Tokmadzic, Sead Islamovic and some others. They said that it was full but that I should try to find a place there and that we would swap our places in this which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you more or less decided to stay in Room 4 based on this discussion that you had with Drago Tokmadzic and the other individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS D
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly describe the conditions in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I think you are moving on to conditions now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I think we have to take the adjournment now. Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is a short matter that I would like to raise. It doesn't need the witness here if he wants to go. It has to do with the public gallery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Witness D, you may leave, return 9.30 tomorrow morning. You are not to discuss your evidence with anybody during the adjournment and that includes members of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Greaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this morning a professional colleague of mine who is instructed as my legal assistant in a case before the Rwanda Tribunal sought to come and sit in the public gallery first thing this morning. As you know, we had a short private session at that time. Because it was in private session, the security told her that she could not sit in the public gallery and if she wanted to watch proceedings, she'd have to go to another court. As a result of which, she wasn't able to realise that the private session came to an end fairly quickly this morning, and was therefore sent off to Court 3 to go off and watch something which she hadn't anticipated seeing. It seems that that's unnecessarily heavy-handed of security to prevent people from waiting until closed session is completed so that they can see the proceedings of this court which, of course, this is not an unimportant trial, and it's certainly important for my client that the public should have proper access to it, and should not be prevented unnecessarily from attending in the public gallery. And if they want to sit here and wait for a closed session to end, then they should be free to do so. As a result she didn't see anything of the proceedings which involves a genocide trial. That is the particular interest that she has and, in my submission, it's to be deprecated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we agree. We'll have the registrar investigate it and report back to us, but in principle, we certainly agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't want to make a terrible fuss about it. It's probably something very simply that can be dealt with quickly and quietly. It just seems to me it ought to be brought to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Vucicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VUCICEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have something I would like to raise in a private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
